summary: RFC 5727 defined processes for the former Real-time Applications and Infrastructure area, including evolution of SIP and related protocols and the operation of the DISPATCH and SIPCORE working groups. This best current practice updates RFC 5727 to allow more flexibility in how such working groups and the SIP change process are run.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a rules update for how a group of engineers decides where new work on a calling protocol should go. The updated rules give them more room to pick what works.

subtitle: Untying the SIP change process from one IETF area, and sharing the DISPATCH way of sorting new work.

tldr.problem: RFC 5727 tied the SIP Change Process to the former RAI area and to the DISPATCH and SIPCORE working groups. When the RAI area merged with the Applications area in 2015, that wording became out of date.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7957 reads references to the RAI area as the cluster of SIP and closely related technologies, and describes 'DISPATCH-style' working groups that any area may adopt to filter new work and choose where it goes.
tldr.outcome: The SIP change rules stay the same while area and working group structure can change. It updates RFC 5727 and is a Best Current Practice.

facts.label: Area merger
facts.value: RAI and APP merged into ART in 2015

today: RFC 7957 is a Best Current Practice that updates RFC 5727; the metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its rules remain in place until a future document changes them.

sections.title: Why RFC 5727 Needed an Update
sections.content:
RFC 5727 described how to evolve and maintain the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) and related technologies in the former Real-time Applications and Infrastructure (RAI) area. These processes are together called the SIP Change Process. Areas do not normally have charters, but RFC 5727 effectively served as one for RAI, and its language was tightly bound to the RAI area and to the DISPATCH and SIPCORE working groups.

In 2015 the RAI area merged with the Applications (APP) area to form the Applications and Real-Time (ART) area. The update removes the dependency on RAI and its working group structure. It does not depend on the names of the new area or any specific working group, since the authors want to future-proof the process against reorganizations.
sections.plainLanguage: The old rulebook named a specific club. When the club merged with another, the rulebook no longer matched. The update rewrites it so club names do not matter.

sections.title: DISPATCH and SIPCORE Roles
sections.content:
Under RFC 5727, the DISPATCH working group assesses potential new work for the area and decides where it should happen. DISPATCH does not take on that new work itself. The SIPCORE working group is responsible for maintaining SIP. Other working groups from the old RAI area develop SIP extensions that do not change the core protocol, new applications of SIP, and other technologies for interactive communication among humans.

This document generalizes the DISPATCH processes so they can be applied to other areas, or to clusters of technologies within an area. It does not change any other aspect of RFC 5727. Areas and working groups may change over time, but the rules for changing SIP and other historically RAI protocols stay the same until a future document updates them.
sections.plainLanguage: One team acts like a front desk that decides who should handle a new request. Another team looks after the main protocol itself. The front desk does not do the work.

sections.title: What a DISPATCH-Style Working Group Does
sections.content:
The DISPATCH working group has proven successful at managing new work for the RAI and ART areas. An area may adopt DISPATCH-like procedures for the whole area or for a technology cluster. The RFC does not recommend this for any specific area other than ART, and leaves the decision to the community and the responsible Area Directors.

A DISPATCH-style group has three essential elements:

  • It evaluates proposals for new work and acts as a filter, deciding whether a proposal is a reasonable use of or addition to the associated technologies. This may rely on established criteria such as the SIP Change Process, on participants' expertise, or both.
  • It chooses a venue. That could be an existing working group, a new BoF or working group (for which it may write a charter), an AD-sponsored individual draft, or a decision not to act at the time.
  • It does not complete the work, though it may adopt milestones to dispatch it, such as charter text, an initial problem statement, or a note on why work was not pursued.
sections.plainLanguage: A DISPATCH-style group sorts new ideas. It checks whether the idea makes sense, then points it to the right team, or says not now. It does not build the idea itself.

sections.title: Limits and Edge Cases
sections.content:
Nothing in the definition stops existing working groups from directly adopting new work that fits their charters, and proposals may go straight to BoF meetings when appropriate. For borderline cases, the responsible Area Directors and chairs decide whether new work starts in a DISPATCH-style group or elsewhere. If an area has several such groups for different purposes or technology clusters, the Area Directors and relevant chairs decide which one handles a proposal.

The charter of a DISPATCH-style group should make that fact clear, either by referencing this document or by directly describing similar procedures.
sections.plainLanguage: The front desk is not mandatory. If a request clearly belongs to one team, it can go straight there, and the grown-ups in charge settle the unclear cases.

sections.title: Decoupling the SIP Change Process from RAI
sections.content:
The RFC clarifies that the SIP Change Process is not bound to any particular area or working group structure. All references to the RAI area in RFC 5727 should be read as "the cluster of SIP and closely related application and infrastructure technologies, as well as other technologies designed primarily for interactive communication, historically among humans".

DISPATCH and SIPCORE are expected to continue in their current capacities, but nothing in the process prevents their responsibilities from being given to other working groups later. All other aspects of the SIP Change Process continue as described in RFC 5727.
sections.plainLanguage: Wherever the old rules said the name of one club, read it as a description of the kind of work. That way the rules still apply even if the club changes names.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document discusses the roles of areas and working groups and creates no new security considerations in the conventional sense. It does point out an organizational risk: a DISPATCH-style group could concentrate control of an area's new work in the hands of far fewer people than the whole area, creating bottlenecks or roadblocks and possibly lowering the quality of decisions about new work.

The best mitigation named is active participation in the group by as many people in the area or cluster as possible.
sections.plainLanguage: If only a few people decide what gets built, they might slow things down or choose badly. The fix is for lots of people to join in and speak up.
